source.title: Deciphering Cultural Representations in Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Chenye Zou; Di-Fan Jiao; Lijie Hu

page_placements.theme: Conditional behavioral control through dictionary features

record.tranche_reason: The study examines cultural features in Gemma-2-9B and Llama-3.1-8B using SAEs and reports representational and intervention results in LLMs, a new setting relative to the toy-model source.
record.gate_note: The study reports SAE feature activations, feature-set similarities, and feature ablations relevant to sparse SAE-recoverable features and their stability. Its steering-performance results are not included: those outputs are deliberately induced, and the table primarily evaluates the study's steering method. The prompt in the appendix is a question-rewriting example, not an instruction addressed to an AI reviewing the paper.
record.test_reason: The study uses existing Gemma Scope and Llama Scope SAEs as a tool to find culture-selective features. It cites superposition and neuron polysemanticity as motivation but never tests them. It does not compare SAE features with neurons, measure how features spread across neurons, check reconstruction or dictionary recovery, or assess whether SAE features are complete or canonical. Its results concern cultural representation: selectivity, paraphrase and format robustness, ablation and steering effects. None bears on whether any version holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors claim SAEs reveal culture-selective features invariant to paraphrase and task format, necessary for cultural reasoning (ablation), and sufficient to modulate it (steering). They call this the first causal evidence that LLMs encode cultural knowledge as decoupled semantic structures. They note limitations: English corpora, survey proxies, SAE reconstruction error, feature splitting, and per-culture tuning of the steering factor.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes pretrained LLM activations with existing SAEs, feature-set similarity, directional ablation, and steering; it does not train toy networks or test superposition geometry as in the original source.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature stability varies by layer: same-culture cross-task similarity is below baseline in early and intermediate layers but exceeds it around Layer 19 and rises in later layers. The ablation study reports a sensitivity spike between Layers 22 and 26.

fits_no_version.finding: Culture-selective SAE features in Gemma-2-9B and Llama-3.1-8B overlap across paraphrases and, in later layers, across QA/Cloze formats. Ablating the top-10 at a mid-depth layer cuts cultural MCQ accuracy from about 0.57 to 0.31; random ablation does not.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLMs encode cultural knowledge in a small set of format-invariant, causally necessary SAE features concentrated at mid-to-late layers.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The evidence concerns cultural representations in a limited set of model families and English-language corpora. The main-text description does not identify the model for several feature-similarity and activation results. No error bars or uncertainty estimates are reported. The text identifies the ablation maximum at Layer 23 but later refers to Layer 25 as the steering turning layer.
record.rows_left_out: The steering-performance comparisons in Table 2 were omitted because steering deliberately induces the cultural output and primarily evaluates the proposed steering method, rather than measuring naturally arising representation or its geometry.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, sparsity transitions or geometry.
All: no capacity or importance analysis.
All: neuron polysemanticity is only asserted via citation.
No measurement of features spread across neurons, and no test of SAE recovery quality or comparison with neurons. SAEs are assumed to work.
No test of completeness, stability across SAE seeds or widths, or canonicality. Feature splitting is noted only as a limitation.
All: no test of feature dimensionality.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' with V4 and V5 supports overreads the study: superposition is cited motivation, and SAEs are an untested tool. The text is internally inconsistent. The top-k for Jaccard is given as 4, 5 and 10 in different places. The turning layer is 23 in Section 6 but 25 in Section 7, and Section 7.1 gives layer 4 for Llama. Most main-text figures do not name the model. Llama ablation results appear only in appendix figures.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, overcomplete sparse features, overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Capacity competition between features, dedicated dimensions for important features, and shared dimensions for others.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.

The study examines cultural features in two LLM families, not whether features generally spread across neurons; it does not compare SAE recovery with neuron-level representations across a broad range of features.
The study measures feature-set stability under paraphrase and task-format changes, but does not establish that SAE features are complete or canonical units.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

relation.reason: SAE decomposition is the analysis tool. The reported tests concern cultural selectivity, prompt invariance, ablation and steering rather than any listed superposition claim version.

tranche.reason: The study uses existing Gemma Scope and Llama Scope SAEs to investigate cultural representations and interventions; it does not independently evaluate superposition, SAE recovery quality, or dictionary canonicality.

source_check.notes: Section 5.2 and Figure 3 disagree on top-5 versus top-10 features; the main-text model for that result is unstated. Random ablation causes marginal or negligible degradation, so the synthesis statement is accurate as a qualitative comparison.
